title: A focused niche and the fit test for choosing one
audience: Teachers, trainers and owners of any service business who are choosing a focus for their offer.
learningOutcomes: Explain how a focused niche narrows the market and makes an offer easier to describe and refer
Score candidate offers against seven fit factors, with an evidence note for each factor marked yes
Reject a candidate that fails the values check, and state the reason in writing

instruction.heading: What a niche does for the business
instruction.body: A niche is a chosen group of clients who share a situation and a result they want, and your offer is designed for that group. Instead of describing a service to everyone, you describe it to people for whom it is the obvious answer. The benefit is clarity. A prospect can tell in one sentence whether you are for them, and a friend can pass your name to the right person. The cost is that you decline some work you could technically do. Make that trade on purpose. A niche is not a promise about income, because income depends on prices, delivery and demand, which the rest of this course covers.

instruction.heading: Weigh the advantages of focus against staying broad
instruction.body: Focus has real advantages. You can draw on experience you already have, clients recognise your real strengths, and the work can sit closer to what you care about. Staying broad has real costs. The message becomes vague, prospects are unsure what you are strongest at, and referrals are harder because people cannot describe you to someone else. Write both lists for your own business before you choose. A focus that gives you no advantage over your current offer is a new label, not a niche.

instruction.heading: Use seven fit factors to compare candidates
instruction.body: List three to five candidate offers. For each one, check how many of seven factors it meets: you are drawn to the work; you feel the offer is genuine when you describe it; it matches your values; it uses your talents; it draws on something particular to you; it builds on experience you have; and it fits a story you can tell honestly. Mark each factor yes, partly or no, and keep a short evidence note beside each yes, such as a past job, a qualification or a client comment. Read the answers as well as the totals. A candidate that scores well on everything except values should be rejected, because a niche you do not believe in tends to wear down.

instruction.heading: Choose a niche you can keep delivering
instruction.body: A niche should be work you can deliver well for years, not only during the first months of enthusiasm. Ask whether you would still choose it after a busy season, a difficult client and a slow month. If the honest answer is no, the candidate has failed, however well it scores on paper. Record the decision, the scores and the date, so that you can later check whether the reasons still hold.

procedure: List three to five candidate offers, one line each
Score each candidate against the seven fit factors as yes, partly or no
Write an evidence note beside every yes, and remove any yes that has no evidence
Reject any candidate that fails the values check, and write the reason
Rank the remaining candidates by their yes marks, then read the reasons behind the top two
Write one sentence that names the group, the need and the offer, and record it with a review date

workedExamples.situation: Owen runs a handyman service in a regional town. He is choosing between 'anything around the house' and 'repairs and fittings for older homes with timber features'. He enjoys restoring old doors and windows and has years of carpentry work behind him.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which candidate should Owen test first, and what evidence should he record?
workedExamples.reasoning: The older-homes candidate meets the drive, talent and experience factors, and it fits a story he can tell honestly. He should test it first and record the scores, the date, and the enquiries from owners of older homes. The sentence should name carpentry as the skill and should not imply any trade licence he does not hold.

workedExamples.situation: A yoga teacher who spent years in office roles considers stretch sessions for desk workers, and a general class for anyone who walks in.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What does the fit test show, and what should she still check?
workedExamples.reasoning: Her office experience and her interest in workplace wellbeing score well. The general class scores low on uniqueness and experience. She should check that the desk-worker offer makes no health promises and that workers or employers will pay for it. The ACCC advertising guide (July 2021) says health and therapeutic claims need reasonable grounds, usually scientific evidence. The result is a candidate, not a decision, until real enquiries arrive.

equipmentAndPpe: No PPE is needed for this lesson
A notebook or spreadsheet for the candidate list and the scores
Your current service list, prices and enquiry records

commonErrors.error: Choosing the candidate with the highest income guess without asking whether you want to do the work
commonErrors.prevention: Apply the values check as a pass or fail test before you look at income.

commonErrors.error: Scoring factors without evidence, so every candidate looks suitable
commonErrors.prevention: For each yes, write one piece of evidence you could show a client.

commonErrors.error: Treating the niche as a slogan rather than a way of working
commonErrors.prevention: Check that your schedule, prices and materials match the niche you have named.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Describing yourself as having specific experience, training or results must be accurate and must not mislead clients. The ACCC's guidance on false or misleading claims is the starting point, but it does not address experience or training claims directly, so check the wider Australian Consumer Law.

Licence notice: this lesson does not cover licensed work and does not grant, confirm or replace any licence. A candidate niche must not be described as licensed work unless you hold the licence that applies in your state or territory. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check with the relevant regulator.

qualityStandard: Each candidate is scored against all seven fit factors, with an evidence note for each yes
Any candidate that fails the values check is recorded as rejected, with the reason
The chosen niche is stated in one sentence that names the group, the need and the offer
documentationEvidence: Candidate list with factor scores and evidence notes
Values check result for each candidate, dated
Chosen niche sentence and its review date
summary: A niche narrows who you serve, so the offer is clear and easy to refer
Weigh the advantages of focus against the cost of staying broad, and decide on purpose
Score candidates on seven fit factors, and let a failed values check overrule a high score
Choose work you can keep delivering, and record the reasons with a review date

knowledgeChecks.question: What does a niche mainly do for a business?
options: It makes the offer clear to a defined group, so people can describe and refer it
It removes the need for a clear price and any need to explain the offer
It stops other people offering similar services in the same area and the same market

knowledgeChecks.question: Two candidate offers score the same on fit. What step should decide between them next?
options: Pick the one with more social media followers and the one with more reviews
Check each against the values test and the evidence for your experience
Choose whichever has the bigger brand name on its page and the bigger logo

knowledgeChecks.question: A candidate scores well on talent and income, but the owner dislikes doing the work. What should happen?
options: Keep it, because a high score settles the matter
Hide the dislike from the clients the business serves
Treat the dislike as a failed check and reconsider the choice
